乎由是上有天之成命也上帝雖難忱而明德
之實自足以昭受之惟德是輔之命至是其成
而不易矣下有治民之休也民心雖難誠而咸
和之化自足以康乂之惟惠是懷之念至是其
集而常保矣蓋申錫無疆天之命由人心而益
固永綏有定民之治因天命而愈周其曰治民
今休不信然乎是則營洛之效皆今日王可自
致者也紹上帝服土中夫固元子之丕任而得
不以自勖哉大抵古之老成謀國未有不篤念
punctuated:
非予小臣之私言也。聞之旦曰：「大邑之作，旣宅土中，以協天地之靈祥，而均四方，以示王者之大公矣。然豈但據其地形已哉？盖王者君臨天下，天之子也，神之依而民之主也。故天非君弗配，則自是可以理陰陽、順四時，而對越乎上天矣；神非類弗歆，則自是可以祀郊社、假祖廟，而饗答乎神祇矣；民非主弗附，則自是可以勤教養、時子惠，而宅中以圖治矣。」若旦之言，固質之吾言不殊焉。其紹上帝、服土中，非王之宜自盡乎？
由是，上有天之成命也。上帝雖難忱，而明德之實自足以昭受之，惟德是輔之命，至是其成而不易矣。下有治民之休也。民心雖難誠，而咸和之化自足以康乂之，惟惠是懷之念，至是其集而常保矣。盖申錫無疆，天之命由人心而益固；永綏有定，民之治因天命而愈周。其曰「治民今休」，不信然乎？是則營洛之效，皆今日王可自致者也。紹上帝、服土中，夫固元子之丕任，而得不以自勗哉！大抵古之老成謀國，未有不篤念
translation_en:
…nor are these merely the private words of your humble servant. I have heard Dan say: “In constructing the great city, we have established the seat at the center of the land, harmonizing with the numinous blessings of Heaven and Earth and giving equal consideration to the four quarters, thereby displaying the sovereign’s perfect impartiality. Yet could this be merely a matter of occupying an advantageous geographical position? The sovereign rules all under Heaven: he is Heaven’s son, the one on whom the spirits depend, and the lord of the people. Heaven has none but the sovereign to serve as its counterpart; hence, from this place, he can regulate yin and yang, bring the four seasons into due order, and reverently respond to Heaven above. The spirits accept offerings only from those of their own kind; hence, from this place, he can offer sacrifices at the suburban altar and the altar of soil, enter the ancestral temple, and requite the spirits of Heaven and Earth with offerings. The people attach themselves to none but their lord; hence, from this place, he can diligently attend to their instruction and sustenance, bestow timely parental kindness, and seek good government while dwelling at the center.” Dan’s words, when compared with mine, surely do not differ. Is it not fitting that the king should devote himself fully to continuing the work of the Lord on High and carrying out his duties at the center of the land?
Thus, above there is Heaven’s established mandate. Although the Lord on High is difficult to rely upon, the substance of radiant virtue is itself sufficient to receive that mandate gloriously. The mandate that supports virtue alone will then be established and remain unchanged. Below there is the excellence of governing the people. Although the people’s hearts are difficult to count upon, the transforming influence of universal harmony is itself sufficient to bring them peace and good order. Their disposition to cherish benevolence alone will then be united and enduringly preserved. With boundless blessings repeatedly bestowed, Heaven’s mandate becomes still more secure through the people’s hearts; with lasting peace firmly established, the government of the people becomes ever more complete through Heaven’s mandate. Is the saying, “The government of the people is now excellent,” not truly so? These, then, are the benefits of establishing Luo, all of which the king can bring about himself today. Continuing the work of the Lord on High and carrying out his duties at the center of the land are indeed the great responsibilities of Heaven’s eldest son. How could he fail to exert himself in fulfilling them? text:
夫天命民心以爲迂治之本者卜洛初定周召
所以戒勉其君何其不謀而皆合也是故曰配
天毖祀卽所以紹上帝矣曰自時中乂卽所以
服行土中矣二公一心無間先後誦其言不可
見乎下文又以敬德祈天進引成王以道事君
之勤何如哉更相輔弼令周室比盛唐虞非偶
然之故矣向使後王後臣皆能用二公佐成王
之道則享國久長豈但過其卜曆已邪

translation_en:
…the Mandate of Heaven and the hearts of the people as the foundation of governance [?]. When the divination establishing Luo as the capital had just been settled, how completely the admonitions and encouragement that the Dukes of Zhou and Shao offered their ruler agreed, though they had not consulted one another! Thus, the words “match Heaven and attend carefully to the sacrifices” express precisely how to carry on the work of the Lord on High; the words “from here govern the central region” express precisely how to discharge one’s duties in the center of the land. The two dukes were of one mind, without any difference between their earlier and later counsel. Can this not be seen by reciting their words? The passage below further guides King Cheng forward by urging him to revere virtue and pray to Heaven. How diligent they were in serving their ruler according to the Way! They assisted him in concert, enabling the house of Zhou to rival the flourishing ages of Tang Yao and Yu Shun; this was no accident. Had subsequent rulers and ministers all been able to follow the way in which the two dukes assisted King Cheng, would the duration of their dynasties merely have exceeded the span foretold by divination?

Book of Odes

“Like the waxing moon, like the rising sun.”
Cheng Guangdian

Associate Examiner Tan, Instructor, comments: He has woven into his essay a comprehensive understanding of the Zhou minister’s wish that his ruler receive great blessings. Is this what is meant by saying that the Odes can stir the feelings?

Associate Examiner Lin, Instructor, comments: The unceasing loyalty and love of a minister for his ruler are exceedingly difficult to convey. This composition unfolds gracefully and reaches into every nuance. It truly captures the poet’s language and meaning and merits inclusion.

Associate Examiner Chen, Director of Studies, comments: By describing the ruler’s blessings through comparison with celestial phenomena, he may be said to have grasped the poet’s skill in expressing praise and prayer.

Examiner Guo, Compiler, comments: He captures the intent of “Heaven Protects” (Tian bao) in invoking blessings upon the ruler.

title: 嘉靖三十一年應天府鄉試錄
text:
考試官右中允尹批忠愛可誦
周臣祝君福之進盛必擬天象以况之焉夫君
福進盛無巳則天下皆蒙其休矣周臣擬天象
而爲况其可以見忠愛之深至與天保之詩臣
受君燕賜歌以申答者也至此若謂吾君獲天
安定旣昭受多福矣神之所以詒貺者又何如
哉擬諸其福吾有取於日月焉夫月之盛皆言
其盈矣抑孰知其生明也不在旣盈之際而在
方恒之時今吾君本一心以熈光明備百順而
===
融高朗不惟如月而巳其諸月之恒者乎蒼哉
生于晦睹懸象之幾望載魄于西見貞明之久
照是恒不終於恒也由恒而進於盈矣夫月以
恒而盈其盈也不可計福以漸而盛其盛也不
可窮福不可窮斯福之至乎此祝君於月者不
取其盈而取其恒者也日之進皆言其中矣抑
孰知其著明也不在旣中之餘而在方升之始
今吾君撫旹治以大明九有秉離德以繼照四
方不徒如日而巳其諸日之升者乎蓋旭日始

周臣祝君福之進盛，必擬天象以况之焉。夫君福進盛無巳，則天下皆蒙其休矣。周臣擬天象而爲况，其可以見忠愛之深至與！天保之詩，臣受君燕賜，歌以申答者也。至此，若謂吾君獲天安定，旣昭受多福矣，神之所以詒貺者又何如哉？擬諸其福，吾有取於日月焉。夫月之盛，皆言其盈矣。抑孰知其生明也，不在旣盈之際，而在方恒之時？今吾君本一心以熈光明，備百順而融高朗，不惟如月而巳，其諸月之恒者乎！蒼哉，生于晦，睹懸象之幾望；載魄于西，見貞明之久照。是恒不終於恒也，由恒而進於盈矣。夫月以恒而盈，其盈也不可計；福以漸而盛，其盛也不可窮。福不可窮，斯福之至乎！此祝君於月者，不取其盈而取其恒者也。日之進，皆言其中矣。抑孰知其著明也，不在旣中之餘，而在方升之始？今吾君撫旹治以大明九有，秉離德以繼照四方，不徒如日而巳，其諸日之升者乎！蓋旭日始
translation_en:
Examiner Yin, Right Companion to the Heir Apparent, comments: “Its loyalty and love merit recitation.”

When the ministers of Zhou wished their ruler blessings of ever-increasing abundance, they invariably likened them to celestial phenomena. For if the ruler’s blessings increase without end, all under Heaven share in their beneficence. In the Zhou ministers’ use of celestial comparisons, can we not discern the depth of their loyalty and love? “Heaven Protects” (Tianbao) is a song sung by ministers in grateful response to their ruler’s gifts at a banquet. At this point, it is as though they were saying: Our ruler has obtained Heaven’s peace and stability and has manifestly received many blessings. Yet what further gifts will the spirits bestow? In seeking comparisons for his blessings, I find them in the sun and moon.

When speaking of the moon’s abundance, everyone speaks of its fullness. Yet who understands that its light is generated not when it is already full, but when it is just beginning to wax? Now our ruler takes his undivided heart as the foundation for spreading radiance, embodies every form of accord, and brings lofty brightness into harmony. He is more than merely like the moon: is he not like the waxing moon? Pale blue [?], it emerges from darkness, and we behold the heavenly image approaching fullness; its dark portion borne in the west [?], we see its constant brightness shining long. This waxing does not end with waxing: from waxing it advances to fullness. As the moon waxes toward fullness, its fullness cannot be measured; as blessings gradually increase, their abundance cannot be exhausted. When blessings cannot be exhausted, is this not their utmost perfection? Thus, in wishing the ruler blessings through the image of the moon, they chose its waxing rather than its fullness.

When speaking of the sun’s advance, everyone speaks of its culmination at noon. Yet who understands that its brightness becomes manifest not after it has reached noon, but when it first begins to rise? Now our ruler presides over an age of good order and brightly illuminates the nine regions; he upholds the virtue of Li, the trigram of brightness, and continuously illuminates the four quarters. He is more than merely like the sun: is he not like the rising sun? For the morning sun has just begun …

translation_en:
…□□□□ the radiance that reaches even the smallest opening; rising at dawn from the Valley of the Sun, it displays its brilliance at midheaven, □□ gazing [?]. This rising does not end with rising: from rising it proceeds to the zenith. The sun reaches the zenith by rising, and none can impede its culmination; blessings become complete through accumulation, and none can thwart their completion. When blessings cannot be thwarted, is this not their fullness? Thus, in invoking the sun to bless the ruler, the poet chooses its rising rather than its culmination. In this way he foretells the descent of divine blessings and hopes that the ruler’s good fortune will never cease. How profound and far-reaching is the loyalty and love of the poet of “Heaven Protects You” (Tian bao)!

Nevertheless, recitation must offer encouragement, and praise must not neglect admonition: this is the foremost duty of a minister serving his ruler. This poem speaks of blessings and prosperity together, yet scarcely mentions his virtue. Why is this? Heaven’s blessings have never come to anyone without □□. How much more must there be a source for the abundant blessings and good fortune that benefit and extend to all the common people! Thus the poet’s subtle intention, left unspoken to the ruler, becomes apparent. Might not later writers who offer compositions but forget admonition within praise, on repeatedly considering this poem, likewise reflect upon “a hundred parts encouragement and one part admonition”?

Tang’s descendant presents his offering and approaches the spirits;
Grant that what we contemplate may be accomplished.
The hand drums and great drums resound deeply;
Clear and shrill are the sounds of the pipes.
Both harmonious and balanced,
They accord with the sound of our stone chimes.
Ah, illustrious descendant of Tang!
Solemn and reverent is his sound.

Gu Mingshi

Comment by Associate Examiner Tan, Instructor: “It is exceedingly difficult to describe how vocal and instrumental music reaches the ancestors. This composition unfolds the Shang people’s performance of music and their communion with the spirits so vividly that one seems to witness it. It deserves to rank first among all the candidates.”

商人述時王獻樂以致神必敘其盛而嘆美之
焉甚矣樂道感通之易也商之後王以獻祭致
神而歎美形於頌聲則樂可觀其深矣想昔商
===
道尚鬼故禮以祭重尚聲故祭以樂尤其宗祀
成湯之詩若謂我商王以成湯之孫承烈祖之
祭奮豫和聲備廟樂於升薦之始致萃孝享接
神明於感格之後以妥以侑盛德自形於俯仰
也八音合而洋洋如在其上焉于豆于登豐功
既象於綴兆也九奏成而勿勿若饗其位焉著
存不忘肅然容聲之有聞因其樂以思其人殆
無遠之不衎也薰蒿既昭流矣乎對越有嚴穆
然慌惚之與交求諸陽而達諸陰殆無幽之弗

商人述時王獻樂以致神，必敘其盛而嘆美之焉。甚矣，樂道感通之易也！商之後王以獻祭致神，而歎美形於頌聲，則樂可觀其深矣。想昔商道尚鬼，故禮以祭重；尚聲，故祭以樂先。其宗祀成湯之詩，若謂我商王以成湯之孫，承烈祖之祭，奮豫和聲，備廟樂於升薦之始；致萃孝享，接神明於感格之後。以妥以侑，盛德自形於俯仰也；八音合，而洋洋如在其上焉。于豆于登，豐功既象於綴兆也；九奏成，而勿勿若饗其位焉。著存不忘，肅然容聲之有聞，因其樂以思其人，殆無遠之不假也。薰蒿既昭，愾矣乎！對越有嚴，穆然慌惚之與交，求諸陽而達諸陰，殆無幽之弗
translation_en:
Associate Examiner Lin, Instructor, comments: Concise and apt, substantial and profound, this piece brings out the music’s tones and meritorious power, seemingly leaving a resonant echo. A masterwork.
Associate Examiner Chen, School Instructor, comments: This piece best captures the profound, ancient style of the hymn Na. It should be recorded as a model.
Examiner Guo, Compiler, comments: Its language and purport are harmonious and balanced.
Examiner Yin, Right Mentor, comments: It vividly depicts the attainment of what is sought in thought.
When the people of Shang described their reigning king presenting music to bring the spirits near, they invariably recounted its magnificence and praised its beauty. How readily the Way of music moves the spirits and establishes communion! The later kings of Shang brought the spirits near through sacrificial offerings, and admiration found expression in hymns of praise: therein one may perceive the profundity of music.
Consider how, in former times, the Way of Shang esteemed spirits, and thus gave sacrifice precedence among rites; it esteemed sound, and thus gave music precedence in sacrifice. Its hymn for the ancestral sacrifice to Cheng Tang seems to say: Our king of Shang, as a descendant of Cheng Tang, carries on the sacrifices to his illustrious ancestor. Rousing joyful and harmonious sounds, he provides the full temple music as the offerings are first raised and presented. Bringing the spirits together through his filial offerings, he communes with the divine powers once his sincerity has moved them to come. As he settles and urges them to partake, his abundant virtue naturally manifests itself in his every bow and movement. The eight classes of instruments sound together, and the spirits seem abundantly present above him. With the offerings in the dou and deng vessels, his great achievements are already represented in the formations of the ritual dancers. The nine musical performances are completed, and the spirits seem to partake at their appointed places, ‘hurriedly’ [?].
Keeping their presence vividly in mind and never forgetting them, he reverently senses their appearance and hears their voices. Through their music he recalls their persons: scarcely any distance is so great that they do not come. Their ascending emanations are already manifest—ah, their very breath! Solemnly facing and attending upon them, he communes in reverent stillness with their elusive presence. He seeks them in the realm of yang and reaches them in the realm of yin: scarcely any recess is so hidden that he does not…

title: 嘉靖三十一年應天府鄉試錄
text:
致也精意其密徹矣乎夫樂道感神之效至是
則聲音之美何如哉盖三闋方舉而鞉皷之播
於革者淵淵乎深以遠焉諸樂始動而管聲之
出於竹者嘒嘒乎清以亮焉律吕和鳴抑揚得
依永之妙作於衆聲者猶夫其磬聲也宫商相
宣清濁適中節之均聞於堂上者猶夫其堂下
也於赫哉我成湯之孫子乎尊祖之念惕然齊
戒之先存故樂行倫清精神自為之滌蕩而美
不可名言矣先祖是聽寧不旣夷懌邪祀先之
===
誠儼然昭假之匪怠故氣召聲比音節自為之
通諧而和無所怗懘矣神保旣格豈復有恫怨
邪夫湯孫以孝祀而形聲樂之美以薦樂而獲
思成之綏孰謂樂道不本於人心哉抑愚於那
頌見商德之不可及矣溫恭之誠在心而其微
能著於樂和平之聲在樂而其幽能達於神要
之一質敬為之本爾非賢聖之君能之乎此正
考父次殷樂章必以那序首而三百篇之肇始
義非無所取之也讀三頌者至是可興起矣

通諧而和無所怗懘矣神保旣格豈復有恫怨

能著於樂和平之聲在樂而其幽能達於神要
之一質敬爲之本爾非賢聖之君能之乎此正
考父次殷樂章必以那序首而三百篇之肇始
義非無所取之也讀三頌者至是可興起矣
punctuated:
致也。精意其密徹矣乎！夫樂道感神之效至是，則聲音之美何如哉？盖三闋方舉，而鞉皷之播於革者，淵淵乎深以遠焉；諸樂始動，而管聲之出於竹者，嘒嘒乎清以亮焉。律吕和鳴，抑揚得依永之妙，作於衆聲者猶夫其磬聲也；宫商相宣，清濁適中節之均，聞於堂上者猶夫其堂下也。於赫哉，我成湯之孫子乎！尊祖之念惕然齊戒之先存，故樂行倫清，精神自為之滌蕩，而美不可名言矣。先祖是聽，寧不旣夷懌邪？祀先之誠儼然昭假之匪怠，故氣召聲比，音節自為之通諧，而和無所怗懘矣。神保旣格，豈復有恫怨邪？夫湯孫以孝祀而形聲樂之美，以薦樂而獲思成之綏，孰謂樂道不本於人心哉？

抑愚於《那》頌見商德之不可及矣。溫恭之誠在心，而其微能著於樂；和平之聲在樂，而其幽能達於神。要之，一質敬為之本爾，非賢聖之君能之乎？此正考父次殷樂章，必以《那》序首，而三百篇之肇始義非無所取之也。讀三頌者至是可興起矣。
translation_en:
…reach. How intimately and thoroughly sincere devotion penetrates! When the Way of music achieves such efficacy in moving the spirits, how beautiful must its sounds be? As the three musical sections are performed, the sounds issuing from the hide of the pellet drums and drums resound deeply and carry far. As the various instruments begin to play, the sounds issuing from the bamboo pipes ring clear and bright. The pitch standards sound in harmony; their rising and falling attain the subtle art of following the sustained singing, and the combined sounds resemble the sound of the stone chimes. The gong and shang notes bring one another forth; the high and low tones attain a balance perfectly suited to the measure, and what is heard above in the hall accords with what is heard below it. How illustrious are we, the descendants of Cheng Tang! The resolve to honor our ancestors is already vigilantly present before purification and fasting begin. Thus, when music is performed and proper relationships are clarified, the spirit is naturally cleansed, and its beauty is beyond words. Hearing this, how could the ancestors fail to be pleased and delighted? The sincerity with which we sacrifice to our forebears is solemn and unremitting in reaching toward them. Thus vital energies summon one another and sounds accord; the musical measures naturally communicate and harmonize, without any discord. Once the protecting spirits have arrived, how could there still be grief or resentment? Through filial sacrifice, Tang’s descendant manifests the beauty of musical sound; through presenting music, he obtains the peace granted when his reverent thoughts attain fulfillment. Who could say that the Way of music is not rooted in the human heart?

Yet I, in my humble judgment, see in the hymn “Na” (How Glorious) that the virtue of Shang cannot be equaled. The sincerity of gentle reverence resides in the heart, yet its subtle workings can become manifest in music; peaceful and harmonious sounds reside in music, yet their hidden efficacy can reach the spirits. In essence, unadorned reverence alone forms their foundation. Could anyone but a worthy and sagely ruler achieve this? This is why, when Zheng Kaofu arranged the musical compositions of Yin, he necessarily placed “Na” first. The significance of beginnings in the three hundred poems likewise has a basis in this. Those who read the three sets of Hymns may, at this point, be stirred to emulation.

text:
春秋
元年春王正月〔隱公元年〕
謝師訓
同考試官教諭盧批體元人能言之用
寅處率多不明此作發揮聖人微旨詳盡取之
考試官修撰郭批得謹嚴體
考試官右中允尹批約傳發經甚明
聖人修經寓王道也述之以明其心作之以明
其政夫心與政王道體用之全也春秋紀元用
===
寅義其有取矣乎且王者居正馭物道本於心
焉自精一執中之傳泯而心之用湮矣春秋于
魯隱卽位之初謂一爲元者若曰元卽仁也仁
不外于心元日元祀典訓之稱在道實一耳聖
人準二儀之化其揆之精矣夫乾坤之道必以
仁而成資始資生之功王者以仁正心則至純
足以周乎理至公足以廣其愛然後正朝廷正
百官正萬民其孰非心之用邪上下同流固王
道之大本大原也天地之元不在我乎是故祖

春秋

元年春王正月。〔隱公元年〕

謝師訓

同考試官教諭盧批：「體元，人能言之；用寅處，率多不明。此作發揮聖人微旨詳盡，取之。」

考試官修撰郭批：「得謹嚴體。」

考試官右中允尹批：「約傳發經甚明。」

聖人修經，寓王道也。述之以明其心，作之以明其政。夫心與政，王道體用之全也。春秋紀元用寅，義其有取矣乎？且王者居正馭物，道本於心焉。自精一執中之傳泯，而心之用湮矣。春秋于魯隱卽位之初，謂一爲元者，若曰元卽仁也。仁不外于心，元日、元祀，典訓之稱，在道實一耳。聖人準二儀之化，其揆之精矣。夫乾坤之道，必以仁而成資始資生之功。王者以仁正心，則至純足以周乎理，至公足以廣其愛，然後正朝廷、正百官、正萬民，其孰非心之用邪？上下同流，固王道之大本大原也。天地之元，不在我乎？是故祖
translation_en:
Spring and Autumn Annals

“First year, spring, the king’s first month.” 〔The first year of Duke Yin.〕

Xie Shixun

Associate Examiner Lu, Instructor, comments: “People can discuss ‘embodying the primal beginning,’ but generally fail to make clear the application of yin. This composition expounds the Sage’s subtle meaning thoroughly and fully. I select it.”

Examiner Guo, Senior Compiler, comments: “It achieves a scrupulous and rigorous style.”

Examiner Yin, Right Rectifier, comments: “It concisely draws on the commentary to elucidate the classic, with great clarity.”

In editing the classic, the Sage embedded within it the Way of kingship. He transmitted it to make clear its guiding mind and composed it to make clear its government. Mind and government together constitute the complete substance and functioning of the Way of kingship. Surely there is significance in the Spring and Autumn Annals’ recording of the primal beginning and its use of yin?

Now, when a king occupies his proper position and governs all things, his Way is rooted in the mind. Once the transmission of the teaching to be discerning and single-minded and to hold fast to the mean disappeared, the functioning of the mind became obscured. At the beginning of Duke Yin of Lu’s reign, the Spring and Autumn Annals calls the first year the ‘primal’ year, as if to say that the primal beginning is benevolence itself. Benevolence does not lie outside the mind. ‘Primal day’ and ‘primal year’ are expressions found in the canonical teachings; in terms of the Way, they are truly one. The Sage took the transforming activity of Heaven and Earth as his standard: how precise his discernment was!

The Way of Heaven and Earth necessarily relies on benevolence to accomplish its work of providing all things with their beginnings and bringing them to life. When a king rectifies his mind through benevolence, his utmost purity suffices to encompass principle, and his utmost impartiality suffices to extend his love broadly. He then rectifies the court, the hundred officials, and the myriad people. Which of these is not a functioning of the mind? Those above and below flowing together is indeed the great foundation and source of the Way of kingship. Does not the primal beginning of Heaven and Earth reside within me? Thus he follows…

title: 嘉靖三十一年應天府鄉試錄
text:
述焉而不變憲章焉而不違首事表年未嘗鑿
智自私而體元之訓將歷萬世無弊也義亦備
矣噫三聖授受道之極致也聖人亦志在春秋
之意歟王者授時成務法寓於政焉自文武成
康之化遠而政之經舛矣春秋于魯隱紀事之
始謂周正爲春者若曰時以作事也時莫善于
寅建丑建子商周之統在法靡同耳聖人酌三
代之禮其從之審矣夫天地之生必以人而建
裁成輔相之業王者正始以寅則時得天下之
正令得天下之善然後和三光順四時齊七政
其孰非人之職邪陰陽各正固王道之大經大
法也裁化之道不在兹乎是故斟酌之而盡變
損益之而盡神定時紀月不敢賊而自專而建
寅之法將更百王不易也旨亦微矣噫爲邦問
答治之準繩也聖人亦見諸行事之驗歟夫至
是則履端正始之法明開物成務之道備而王
道於是乎出焉抑春秋大一統聖人不敢改正
朔立制度所以尊君父定大倫蓋百世綱常之

punctuated: 述焉而不變，憲章焉而不違，首事表年，未嘗鑿智自私，而體元之訓將歷萬世無弊也，義亦備矣。噫！三聖授受，道之極致也。聖人亦志在《春秋》之意歟？王者授時成務，法寓於政焉。自文武成康之化遠，而政之經舛矣。《春秋》于魯隱紀事之始，謂周正爲春者，若曰時以作事也。時莫善于寅，建丑、建子，商周之統，在法靡同耳。聖人酌三代之禮，其從之審矣。夫天地之生，必以人而建裁成輔相之業。王者正始以寅，則時得天下之正，令得天下之善，然後和三光，順四時，齊七政，其孰非人之職邪？陰陽各正，固王道之大經大法也。裁化之道不在兹乎？是故斟酌之而盡變，損益之而盡神，定時紀月，不敢賊而自專，而建寅之法將更百王不易也，旨亦微矣。噫！爲邦問答，治之準繩也。聖人亦見諸行事之驗歟？夫至是，則履端正始之法明，開物成務之道備，而王道於是乎出焉。抑《春秋》大一統，聖人不敢改正朔、立制度，所以尊君父、定大倫，蓋百世綱常之
translation_en:
…continued their legacy without altering it and took their institutions as a model without departing from them. In marking the beginning of events and designating the year, he never contrived clever innovations for private ends. The teaching of embodying the primal beginning would thus endure for ten thousand generations without defect: its meaning was fully expressed. Ah! The transmission and reception among the three sages represent the highest attainment of the Way. Was this also what the Sage intended in the Spring and Autumn Annals?

The true king establishes the calendar and brings affairs to completion; standards are embodied in his government. Once the transforming influence of Kings Wen, Wu, Cheng, and Kang had receded into the distant past, the guiding principles of government became disordered. At the beginning of its record of events under Duke Yin of Lu, the Spring and Autumn Annals calls the first month of the Zhou calendar “spring,” as if to say that the seasons serve to initiate undertakings. For the calendar, nothing is better than beginning the year with the month designated yin. Beginning it with chou or zi belonged respectively to the calendrical systems of Shang and Zhou: their rules simply differed. The Sage weighed the rites of the Three Dynasties and carefully considered which to follow.

The generative activity of Heaven and Earth necessarily relies on human beings to undertake the work of regulating and completing it, assisting and supporting it. When the true king rectifies the year's beginning by adopting yin, the calendar attains the proper standard for all under Heaven, and ordinances attain what is best for all under Heaven. Thereupon he brings the three luminaries into harmony, accords with the four seasons, and coordinates the seven celestial regulators. Which of these is not a human responsibility? For yin and yang each to occupy its proper position is indeed a cardinal principle and great rule of the Kingly Way. Does not the way of regulating transformation lie here? Thus he weighs alternatives so as to encompass every adaptation, and makes reductions and additions so as to realize the full subtlety of their operation. In fixing the seasons and recording the months, he dares not impair the proper order by acting on his own authority. The rule of beginning the year with yin would therefore remain unchanged through the succession of a hundred kings: its purport is indeed profound. Ah! The question and answer about governing a state are the standard for good government. Was this also the practical verification that the Sage sought to manifest through events?

At this point, the rule for proceeding from the first moment and rectifying the beginning becomes clear, and the way of opening things to fulfillment and bringing affairs to completion is complete; from this the Kingly Way emerges. Yet the Spring and Autumn Annals prizes unified rule. The Sage dared not change the calendrical beginning of the year or establish institutions: thereby he honored ruler and father and firmly established the fundamental human relationships. For this is that upon which the cardinal bonds and constant norms of a hundred generations…

text:
也敦本厚族在事則有義也倫以天秩而所制
有等級之殊義本人爲而所施有先後之序是
以葛藟之次揚水之譏詩有明徵焉何晋平徒
勤厚母之愛罔知敦族之本其視諸先世之光
烈固有成憲可以爲監者也急于城杞何爲者
耶晋主夏盟令行中國率五侯九伯之職以伸
尊獎王室之義非一日矣如文如襄如悼之業
非平之所當嗣守者乎是故文自城濮勝楚之
後荷天王下勞之禮而講踐土之盟當是時六
===
飛至止虎賁來三百之錫作宫衡雍出入展三
覲之誠尊獎之大義昭申于同好之國天子之
休命對揚于肆覲之時人謂晋之此盟信也德
攻也伯業固造端于此矣嗣是而襄公旣祥之
後怒衛之不朝且侵虐隣境也乃聲其罪于諸
侯而致伐焉其聽且居之言修于溫之覲重輕
有禮襄固知所本矣於戲忠敬之心達而天威
不違于咫尺臣子之分肅而父功克纘于禮文
卒之戚田奏績昭子告獲非效尤以長亂者斯

…such are the ordered relationships. Strengthening the roots and treating one’s clan generously are matters of duty in the conduct of affairs. Relationships follow Heaven’s ordering, and their regulation distinguishes degrees and ranks; duty is grounded in human action, and its exercise has an order of precedence. Thus the placement of “Gelei” and the criticism in “Yangshui” [?] provide clear testimony in the Book of Odes. Why did Duke Ping of Jin devote himself merely to affectionate care for his mother, without understanding the fundamental importance of strengthening his clan? Looking to the illustrious achievements of his predecessors, he certainly had established precedents that could serve as a mirror. What, then, was he doing in his haste to fortify Qi?

Jin had long presided over the covenants of the central states, and its commands held sway throughout them. It led the regional lords in fulfilling their duties, thereby upholding the obligation to honor and support the royal house. Were not the achievements of Dukes Wen, Xiang, and Dao precisely what Duke Ping ought to have inherited and preserved? Thus, after defeating Chu at Chengpu, Duke Wen received the Heavenly King’s gracious ceremonial recognition and convened the covenant at Jiantu. At that time the royal six-horse chariot arrived, and a gift of three hundred Tiger Guards was bestowed. A palace was built at Hengyong, and through his comings and goings Duke Wen displayed his sincerity in three royal audiences. The great obligation to honor and support the throne was manifestly upheld among the allied states, and the Son of Heaven’s gracious commands were acknowledged and extolled at the formal audience. People said of this covenant of Jin that it was trustworthy and that it was an achievement of virtue [?]. The enterprise of hegemony indeed began here.

Thereafter, once Duke Xiang had performed the concluding mourning sacrifice, he was angered that Wei failed to attend his court and also invaded and maltreated neighboring territories. He therefore proclaimed its offenses to the regional lords and launched an attack. Yet he heeded Juju’s words and performed the royal audience at Wen, observing ritual propriety in assigning greater and lesser importance to his obligations. Xiang certainly understood what was fundamental. Ah! His loyal and reverent heart found expression, and Heaven’s majesty remained close at hand; his observance of the duties of subject and son was solemn, and through ritual forms he successfully continued his father’s achievements. Finally, the hunt at Qi yielded results, and Zhaozi reported the game taken. He was no imitator of wrongdoing who thereby fostered disorder; this…

title: 嘉靖三十一年應天府鄉試錄
text:
□□襄之九年又若悼公因鄭人之反覆不
恒也乃大合十二國之諸侯伐之而同盟于亳
城北焉其威加四境之後共申尊奬之義終始
一德悼亦知所本矣於戲司愼司盟忠愛之念
質諸神明而不爽救災恤患好惡之公率彼同
好而無二卒之鄭人恐懼以行成諸侯恊心以
聽命三駕成而功收二十四年之好者斯不爲
伯業之盛乎是則文也襄也悼也皆能尊奬王
室以恤宗周之闕而平繼其後獨不能光昭舊
===
業而夏肄是屏輕棄諸姬有愧于先德多矣故
春秋書三公之績而美惡之勸戒彰彰也抑平
之不競不但是也盟溴梁而贅旒之勢成會沙
隨而待下之禮薄甚至從交相見諸侯南向而
朝楚宋財一歸縱釋有罪而不討其于夷夏之
防輕重之分曾有一於舉乎嗚呼伯道之興王
道之衰也況後人之不能守業者邪聖人傷平
之顛而嘉文襄悼之功不得已也于是乎見待

punctuated:
□□。襄之九年，又若悼公因鄭人之反覆不恒也，乃大合十二國之諸侯伐之，而同盟于亳城北焉。其威加四境之後，共申尊奬之義，終始一德，悼亦知所本矣。於戲！司愼司盟，忠愛之念質諸神明而不爽；救災恤患，好惡之公率彼同好而無二。卒之鄭人恐懼以行成，諸侯恊心以聽命，三駕成而功收二十四年之好者，斯不爲伯業之盛乎？是則文也、襄也、悼也，皆能尊奬王室，以恤宗周之闕，而平繼其後，獨不能光昭舊業，而夏肄是屏，輕棄諸姬，有愧于先德多矣。故《春秋》書三公之績，而美惡之勸戒彰彰也。
抑平之不競，不但是也。盟溴梁而贅旒之勢成，會沙隨而待下之禮薄，甚至從交相見，諸侯南向而朝楚，宋財一歸，縱釋有罪而不討。其于夷夏之防、輕重之分，曾有一於舉乎？嗚呼！伯道之興，王道之衰也，況後人之不能守業者邪？聖人傷平之顛，而嘉文、襄、悼之功，不得已也。于是乎見待衰世之意與望盛世之心。
translation_en:
…[Two illegible characters.] Again, in the ninth year of Duke Xiang of Lu, Duke Dao of Jin, because the people of Zheng repeatedly changed sides and lacked constancy, assembled the lords of twelve states in a great coalition to attack Zheng, and together they entered into a covenant north of Bocheng. After his might had reached the four borders, they jointly reaffirmed their obligation to honor and support the royal house, remaining constant in their virtue from beginning to end. Duke Dao, too, understood the foundation of his undertaking. Ah! Before the spirits who oversee vigilance and covenants, their loyal and devoted intentions were pledged without deviation. In relieving disasters and aiding those in distress, their impartial judgments of whom to favor and oppose guided their allies without wavering. Ultimately, the people of Zheng, in fear, sought peace, and the feudal lords obeyed his commands with one accord. Three campaigns succeeded, securing twenty-four years of amicable relations. Was this not the flourishing of hegemonic achievement? Thus Dukes Wen, Xiang, and Dao all honored and supported the royal house, making good the deficiencies of the Zhou court. Yet Duke Ping, who succeeded them, alone failed to glorify their inherited achievements. Instead, he cast aside the surviving offshoot of Xia and lightly abandoned the states of the Ji lineage. In many respects he fell shamefully short of his predecessors’ virtue. Thus the Spring and Autumn Annals records the achievements of the three dukes, making abundantly clear its encouragement of good and admonition against evil.
Yet Duke Ping’s weakness was not confined to this. At the covenant at Jueliang [?], his position became that of a mere pendant hanging from a banner; at the meeting at Shasui, he showed scant ritual courtesy toward his subordinates. Matters even reached the point of reciprocal meetings [?], with the feudal lords facing south to pay court to Chu. Once wealth from Song was delivered, he released the guilty without punishing them. In maintaining the boundary between the Yi peoples and the Xia states, or distinguishing matters of greater and lesser importance, did he ever accomplish even one thing? Alas! The rise of the way of the hegemon was itself the decline of the way of the true king. How much worse when later rulers could not even preserve their inherited achievements! The Sage lamented Duke Ping’s downfall and commended the achievements of Dukes Wen, Xiang, and Dao because he had no alternative. Here we see his intention in dealing with an age of decline and his heartfelt hope for an age of flourishing.

Record of Rites

“When the Three Kings sacrificed to the waterways, they all placed the Yellow River before the sea: the one was the source, the other the gathering place of the waters. This is called attending to the root.”

Lu Yifeng 陸一鳯

Comment by Associate Examiner Zhou, Instructor: “The topic itself is clear and is not difficult to write on. But most examination scripts fail to bring out clearly the point about attending to the root. This essay alone uses words economically while making its meaning spring vividly forth; hence its inclusion.”

Comment by Examiner Guo, Senior Compiler: “Clear and fluent.”

Comment by Examiner Yin, Right Assistant Mentor: “The writing has vigor.”

The Record sets forth [?] the meaning of the order in which successive dynasties sacrificed to the waterways, showing that learning prizes the root. In sacrificing to the waterways, the Three Kings placed the Yellow River first: they did not put the root last. Can we not thereby see that learning prizes the root [?]? Such is the meaning of the “Record of Learning.” Why is this so? The principles of the world have roots and branches, and the gentleman’s learning has its proper sequence. We may infer this simply by considering the Three Kings’ sacrifices to the waterways.

Thus, the hundred rivers are all notable waters of the realm, yet there must be great waterways to receive and gather their many currents. The Yellow River within and the sea without are indeed the framework of the Nine Provinces, defining the extent and bounds of their territory. The hundred spirits are all those to whom the Son of Heaven should offer sacrifice, yet there must be an ordered sacrificial system to requite the benefits bestowed by the waters. Placing the Yellow River first and the sea afterward was indeed the established practice of the Three Kings, governing the presentation of offerings at the appointed seasons of the year.

title: 嘉靖三十一年應天府鄉試錄
text:
後海矣三王之祭必先之要非無義之存者誠
以河居海之上流在川則爲源焉源之所出其
祭之所以先乎海之爲物其巨不知凡幾河矣
三代之祭必後之殆非反禮之正者誠以海受
河之下流在川則爲委焉委之所聚其祭之所
以後乎故由先後之祭以求源委之義則河之
先祭非私於河也川始於源祭不得不先之也
君子觀盈科之進可以見水之本矣而謂學不
有似之邪因源委之義以察本末之務則海之
===
後祭非薄於海也川終為委祭不得不後之也
君子務成章之達可以識學之本矣而謂學不
有同乎水邪是則祭有先後之倫河海知所分
則委大不以加源而祭之道得矣學有緩急之
序本末知所辨則末緩不以先本而學之務明
矣君子察此庶幾志學之有其端與抑學記一
書大抵多明務本之義其古大學教人之遺法
邪蓋始教七倫無非求心之要然必以循序漸
進爲功則古人之爲學可識矣求諸大學至善

punctuated: 後海矣。三王之祭必先之，要非無義之存者，誠以河居海之上流，在川則爲源焉。源之所出，其祭之所以先乎？海之爲物，其巨不知凡幾河矣。三代之祭必後之，殆非反禮之正者，誠以海受河之下流，在川則爲委焉。委之所聚，其祭之所以後乎？故由先後之祭，以求源委之義，則河之先祭，非私於河也；川始於源，祭不得不先之也。君子觀盈科之進，可以見水之本矣，而謂學不有似之邪？因源委之義，以察本末之務，則海之後祭，非薄於海也；川終為委，祭不得不後之也。君子務成章之達，可以識學之本矣，而謂學不有同乎水邪？是則祭有先後之倫，河海知所分，則委大不以加源，而祭之道得矣；學有緩急之序，本末知所辨，則末緩不以先本，而學之務明矣。君子察此，庶幾志學之有其端與？抑《學記》一書，大抵多明務本之義，其古大學教人之遺法邪？蓋始教七倫，無非求心之要，然必以循序漸進爲功，則古人之爲學可識矣。求諸《大學》，至善
translation_en:
…the sea that follows it [?]. In their sacrifices, the Three Kings invariably gave the Yellow River precedence. Surely this was not without a meaningful principle: the Yellow River lies upstream from the sea and, among the waterways, serves as the source. Is not its position as the source from which the waters emerge the reason it receives sacrifice first? As for the sea, its vastness exceeds that of the Yellow River by an incalculable amount. Yet the sacrifices of the Three Dynasties invariably placed it afterward. This surely did not contravene proper ritual: the sea receives the Yellow River’s downstream waters and, among the waterways, serves as their destination. Is not its position as the destination where the waters gather the reason it receives sacrifice afterward?

Thus, if we seek the meaning of source and destination through the order of sacrifices, we see that sacrificing first to the Yellow River is no act of partiality toward it. Waterways begin at their source, so sacrifice must give it precedence. By observing how water fills each hollow before advancing, the gentleman can perceive the foundation of water’s progress. Can one then say that learning bears no resemblance to it? If we examine the tasks pertaining to root and branch through the meaning of source and destination, we see that sacrificing afterward to the sea does not slight it. Waterways end at their destination, so sacrifice must place it afterward. By striving to advance only after completing a coherent stage of learning, the gentleman can recognize learning’s foundation. Can one then say that learning has nothing in common with water?

Sacrifice thus has its proper order of precedence. When the distinction between river and sea is understood, the destination, though vast, is not elevated above the source, and the proper way of sacrifice is attained. Learning likewise has an order of lesser and greater urgency. When root and branch are properly distinguished, the branches, being less urgent, are not put before the root, and the task of learning becomes clear. If the gentleman examines this, might he come close to finding the proper starting point for his resolve to learn?

Moreover, the Record of Learning, taken as a whole, repeatedly elucidates the principle of attending to the root. Might it preserve the methods by which the ancient institutions of higher learning taught people? The seven principles governing the commencement of instruction [?] are all essentials for seeking one’s heart; yet accomplishment necessarily depends on proceeding gradually and in order. From this, we can understand how the ancients pursued learning. If we look to the Great Learning, the highest good…

title: 嘉靖三十一年應天府鄉試錄
text:
之止必始於格物格物之功必要於知本故曰
物有本末事有終始知所先後則近道矣茲非
其序乎後之學者遺本於求心乃欲棄漸進以
馳騖乎高遠噫讀此不可少喻也哉
是故清明象天廣大象地終始象四時周
還象風雨
王京祥
同考試官教諭周批樂象造化題有分
貼精確無如此作
===
考試官修撰郭批說有理致
考試官右中允尹批整實
記者詳樂之制而擬諸造化焉夫法象莫大乎
造化也樂制與之準焉其取類不亦大哉昔者
記樂之言曰樂也者本於身之順正者也發諸
德之光動氣之和而萬物之理著矣其擬諸
造化何如哉是故輕清高明天道之運也樂非
天也其聲之清明則象焉吾見純然不雜其諧
暢通之神皦然不亂猶之昭明之著天以一元氣

之止，必始於格物；格物之功，必要於知本。故曰：「物有本末，事有終始，知所先後，則近道矣。」茲非其序乎？後之學者遺本於求心，乃欲棄漸進以馳騖乎高遠。噫！讀此，不可少喻也哉？

是故清明象天，廣大象地，終始象四時，周還象風雨。

王京祥

同考試官教諭周批：樂象造化，題有分貼，精確無如此作。

考試官修撰郭批：說有理致。

考試官右中允尹批：整實。

記者詳樂之制，而擬諸造化焉。夫法象莫大乎造化也，樂制與之準焉，其取類不亦大哉？昔者記樂之言曰：「樂也者，本於身之順正者也。」發諸德之光，動氣之和，而萬物之理著矣。其擬諸造化何如哉？是故輕清高明，天道之運也。樂非天也，其聲之清明則象焉。吾見純然不雜，其諧暢通之神；皦然不亂，猶之昭明之著。天以一元氣
translation_en:
…abiding in the highest good must begin with investigating things; the work of investigating things must take knowing the root as its essential aim. Thus it is said: “Things have roots and branches; affairs have endings and beginnings. To know what comes first and what comes afterward is to approach the Way.” Is this not the proper sequence? Later students neglect the root in seeking the mind, and would abandon gradual progress to pursue what is lofty and remote. Alas! Can reading this fail to bring them even a little understanding?

“Thus, its clarity and brightness resemble Heaven; its breadth and greatness resemble Earth; its endings and beginnings resemble the four seasons; its cyclical recurrence resembles wind and rain.”

Wang Jingxiang

Comment by Associate Examiner Zhou, Instructor: “Music resembles the creative transformations of nature. The topic has distinct aspects, each requiring appropriate treatment; no other composition matches this one in precision.”

Comment by Examiner Guo, Senior Compiler: “The exposition has reasoned depth.”

Comment by Examiner Yin, Right Mentor of the Heir Apparent: “Orderly and substantial.”

The author of the Record explains the structure of music in detail and compares it to the creative transformations of nature. Nothing is greater than these transformations as a model, and the structure of music accords with them. Is the analogy it draws not grand indeed? The ancient account of music says: “Music is rooted in the harmony and rectitude of one’s person.” It issues from the radiance of virtue and sets in motion the harmony of vital energy, making manifest the principles of all things. How, then, does it resemble the creative transformations of nature?

Lightness and purity, loftiness and brightness: these characterize the operation of Heaven’s Way. Music is not Heaven, yet in the clarity and brightness of its sounds it resembles Heaven. I see its purity, free of admixture—the wondrous efficacy of its harmonious, unimpeded flow; its distinctness, free of disorder—like the manifestation of celestial brightness. Heaven, by means of a single primal vital energy…

title: 嘉靖三十一年應天府鄉試錄
text:
成其化樂以元聲召其和清明非所以象天乎
廣博遠大地載之神也樂非地也其體之廣大
則象焉吾見凝精粗之體即翕受而能容極情
文之備一博厚而兼載地盡其物而無外樂盡
其數而無餘廣大非所以象地乎以至起于黃
鐘終于仲呂樂有所謂終始也條理順布有四
時之象焉倡焉而無不通則始也者春夏之象
也和焉而無不復則終也者秋冬之象也天以
時而成歲樂以順而合倫其異道而同序者乎
===
故曰終始者象四時者也作之以柷止之以敔
樂有所謂周旋也律呂宣應有風雨之象焉上
下相生之理一陰陽之散潤也迭相爲經之道
一風雨之奮蕩也風雨播降之有時樂則聲振
之有度其殊氣而同節者乎故曰周還者象風
雨者也是則象乎天地與天地合其德矣象乎
四時與四時合其序矣象乎風雨與陰陽合其
變化矣一舉樂而造化之大胥備焉君子曰樂
觀其深信夫大抵樂之道禮所出也先王防僞

punctuated: 成其化，樂以元聲召其和，清明非所以象天乎？廣博遠大，地載之神也。樂非地也，其體之廣大則象焉。吾見凝精粗之體，即翕受而能容；極情文之備，一博厚而兼載。地盡其物而無外，樂盡其數而無餘，廣大非所以象地乎？以至起于黃鐘，終于仲呂，樂有所謂終始也。條理順布，有四時之象焉。倡焉而無不通，則始也者，春夏之象也；和焉而無不復，則終也者，秋冬之象也。天以時而成歲，樂以順而合倫，其異道而同序者乎？故曰：「終始者，象四時者也。」作之以柷，止之以敔，樂有所謂周旋也。律呂宣應，有風雨之象焉。上下相生之理，一陰陽之散潤也；迭相爲經之道，一風雨之奮蕩也。風雨播降之有時，樂則聲振之有度，其殊氣而同節者乎？故曰：「周還者，象風雨者也。」是則象乎天地，與天地合其德矣；象乎四時，與四時合其序矣；象乎風雨，與陰陽合其變化矣。一舉樂而造化之大胥備焉。君子曰：「樂觀其深。」信夫！大抵樂之道，禮所出也。先王防僞
translation_en: …accomplishes its transformations, while music summons harmony through its fundamental sound. Is not its clarity and brightness how it images Heaven? Breadth, reach, and vastness are the wondrous power by which Earth bears all things. Music is not Earth, yet the breadth and vastness of its form image Earth. I see it bringing together the refined and the coarse into one body, receiving and accommodating them all; encompassing the fullness of feeling and patterned expression, it bears everything with the same breadth and depth. Earth embraces all its things, leaving nothing outside; music exhausts all its numerical relations, leaving nothing over. Is not its breadth and vastness how it images Earth? Furthermore, beginning with Huangzhong and ending with Zhonglü, music has what are called its endings and beginnings. Its ordered patterns unfold harmoniously, imaging the four seasons. When a leading note sounds and everything flows freely, this beginning images spring and summer; when answering notes sound and everything returns, this ending images autumn and winter. Heaven completes the year through the seasons; music brings its relations into accord through harmonious succession. Do they not follow different courses yet share the same order? Thus it is said: “Endings and beginnings image the four seasons.” Music is begun with the zhu, a wooden percussion box, and stopped with the yu, a scraped wooden instrument: music has what is called its cyclical movement. The yang and yin pitch standards sound forth and respond, imaging wind and rain. The principle by which pitches generate one another upward and downward is one with the dispersing and moistening action of yin and yang; the way they take turns as the governing standard is one with the stirring and sweeping action of wind and rain. Wind and rain spread and descend at their proper times; musical sounds likewise resound according to measure. Do they not differ in their vital forces yet share the same regulation? Thus it is said: “Cyclical return images wind and rain.” Thus, in imaging Heaven and Earth, music accords with their potency; in imaging the four seasons, it accords with their succession; in imaging wind and rain, it accords with the transformations of yin and yang. In a single performance of music, the full grandeur of creation is present. The gentleman says: “In music, observe its depth.” How true! Broadly speaking, the Way of music issues from ritual propriety. The former kings guarded against deception…

title: 嘉靖三十一年應天府鄉試錄
text:
以禮而民斯中防情以樂而民斯和故制禮法
修教化使三綱正九疇叙天下化中然後作樂
以宣八風之氣平萬物之情此禮先樂後治道
之所由成也君子反情比類修其身而禮樂興
則中和在我所以位天地育萬物神化之妙有
出乎象器之外者矣漢志曰天子建中和之極
兼總條貫金聲而玉振之斯言也庶幾達禮樂
之本
第貳場
===
論
禮者聖人之成法
張溥
同考試官教諭張批禮之原在心措之
天下而治法道法一以貫之惟聖人能然張子
立說閎闊令人猝難理會故作者各據一偏造
詞失其本旨惟此篇善檃括題要妙意匠於規
矩之中出巧法於繩墨之外其可為文之式巳
允宜首薦

translation_en:
…through ritual, and the people thereby attain balance; they restrain the emotions through music, and the people thereby attain harmony. Thus they establish ritual rules and cultivate moral instruction, ensuring that the Three Bonds are correct, the Nine Categories are ordered, and all under Heaven are transformed toward balance. Only then do they make music, to disseminate the vital energies of the eight winds and bring equilibrium to the dispositions of all things. Ritual comes first and music afterward: this is how the Way of governance is accomplished. The gentleman examines his emotions, compares analogous things, and cultivates himself, so that ritual and music flourish. Balance and harmony then reside within him, enabling Heaven and Earth to take their proper places and all things to be nourished. The subtle efficacy of spiritual transformation extends beyond perceptible forms and material instruments. The Treatise in the History of the Han states: “The Son of Heaven establishes the supreme standard of balance and harmony, comprehensively unites its guiding principles, and brings them to fulfillment, as bells sound and jade chimes complete the music.” These words come close to comprehending the foundation of ritual and music.
Second Session
Discourse
“Ritual is the established model of the sages.”
Zhang Pu
Comment by Associate Examiner Zhang, Instructor: The source of ritual lies in the heart; when applied throughout the realm, it produces order. Its models and the models of the Way are bound together by a single principle [?]; only a sage can accomplish this. Master Zhang’s formulation is so expansive that it is difficult to grasp at once. Consequently, the writers each composed their arguments from a partial perspective and missed his original intent. This essay alone skillfully encapsulates the essentials of the topic. It displays marvelous ingenuity within the prescribed rules and devises skillful methods beyond their bounds. Surely it can serve as a model for composition! It fully deserves to be recommended first.

Comment by Associate Examiner Chen, Instructor: The sage takes formless ritual propriety as his foundation and brings forth established models. In applying them as circumstances require and attaining the mean appropriate to the time, he invariably puts this same thing into operation. Master Zhang’s argument is clear in its purport. The candidates in the examination hall have failed to grasp his meaning; most indulge freely in empty rhetoric, leaving readers bewildered. This essay encompasses almost the entire meaning of the topic. With its rises and falls, pauses and turns, it achieves literary distinction without striving for ornament. Surely its author is a man of accumulated learning and discernment! Who could say it inappropriate to place him ahead of the other candidates?

title: 嘉靖三十一年應天府鄉試錄
text:
虚虚之謂無本禮非文則僣僣之謂無用無本
不立無用不行聖人全其體而會其用者也定
物以裁化協中以盡神因理出文以品節持防
夫斯世則百姓與中與能之道在我矣由是斟
酌損益通其變以宜乎民協諸時中立萬世常
行之極則天下之人心得所守以反其性而入
於治也不難矣故曰禮者聖人之成法也子張
子其可謂達禮之要乎夫禮者天地之經也人
物之紀也治亂存亡之所從出可終身由而不
===
可斯須去身者也道在天地流行乎一氣渾淪
磅礴其理一而已理原於一本散於萬殊其所
以合天地明日月序四時著星辰行江河峙山
嶽蕃品物者合而至章動而至神天地之自然
禮之體也宰世馭物經紀明時高卑升降之有
等遠邇疎戚之有别文質兼施而無過不及經
權並用而有變有常天敘天秩井然煥然以成
天下之治者萬事之當然禮之用也無體之本
出于心成于其性而有用之妙發于事着于為

punctuated: 虚，虚之謂無本；禮非文則僣，僣之謂無用。無本不立，無用不行。聖人全其體而會其用者也，定物以裁化，協中以盡神，因理出文，以品節持防夫斯世，則百姓與中與能之道在我矣。由是斟酌損益，通其變以宜乎民，協諸時中，立萬世常行之極，則天下之人心得所守，以反其性而入於治也不難矣。故曰：「禮者，聖人之成法也。」子張子其可謂達禮之要乎！夫禮者，天地之經也，人物之紀也，治亂存亡之所從出，可終身由而不可斯須去身者也。道在天地，流行乎一氣，渾淪磅礴，其理一而已。理原於一本，散於萬殊，其所以合天地、明日月、序四時、著星辰、行江河、峙山嶽、蕃品物者，合而至章，動而至神，天地之自然，禮之體也。宰世馭物，經紀明時，高卑升降之有等，遠邇疎戚之有别，文質兼施而無過不及，經權並用而有變有常，天敘天秩，井然煥然，以成天下之治者，萬事之當然，禮之用也。無體之本，出于心，成于其性，而有用之妙，發于事，着于為
translation_en: …empty; emptiness means having no foundation. Without patterned forms, ritual becomes presumptuous; presumption means having no practical function. Without a foundation it cannot stand; without practical function it cannot operate. The sage fully realizes its substance and comprehends its application. He settles things so as to regulate transformation, accords with the mean so as to exhaust the workings of the numinous, and brings forth patterned forms in accordance with principle. Through these he establishes measured distinctions and maintains safeguards for this world. Thus the way by which the common people attain the mean and fulfill their capacities lies with him. Accordingly, he weighs additions and reductions and comprehends changes so as to suit the people, conforming to the mean appropriate to the time and establishing the supreme standard to be practiced constantly for myriad generations. Then the hearts of all people under Heaven will have something to hold fast to, and it will not be difficult for them to return to their nature and enter into good order. Thus it is said: “Ritual is the established model of the sages.” May Master Zhang not be said to have understood the essentials of ritual! Ritual is the constant framework of Heaven and Earth, the ordering principle of people and things, and that upon which order and disorder, survival and destruction depend. One must follow it throughout one’s life and cannot depart from it even for an instant. The Way exists in Heaven and Earth, flowing through the single vital energy, undivided and all-pervading; its principle is simply one. Principle originates in a single root and disperses into myriad particular manifestations. Through it Heaven and Earth are joined, the sun and moon shine, the four seasons proceed in order, the stars appear, rivers flow, mountains stand, and the various kinds of things multiply. United, it is supremely manifest; in movement, it is supremely numinous. This is the spontaneous order of Heaven and Earth, the substance of ritual. Governing the world and directing things, ordering an enlightened age, establishing grades of high and low, ascent and descent, and distinctions between near and far, distant and close relations; employing patterned forms and substance together without excess or deficiency; applying both constant norms and discretionary judgment, with both change and constancy; bringing Heaven’s ordering and Heaven’s ranks into orderly and brilliant array so as to achieve good government throughout the world: these are what ought to obtain in all affairs, the application of ritual. The foundation of the formless substance [?] issues from the heart and is completed in one’s nature, while the subtle efficacy of its application emerges in affairs and becomes manifest in doing…

作言行之間協于因時處中之極以辨朝廷以
肅宗廟以殿邦國以施鄉黨使天下由其理以
不畔循其文以不變立綱陳紀輕重同得後可
以垂於無窮禮之品節文章也若夫寒暑愆期
四時失序山川崩竭飛植折夭人倫乖亂法紀
紛張異說横行强暴交作此禮之大壞極弊動

内外持養中和兼致合天地于一體會人物于

新之會而弗逆于時通變易之宜而弗矯于化

…in actions, words, and conduct, accord with the highest standard of adapting to the times and abiding in the mean: distinguishing ranks at court, bringing solemn order to the ancestral temples, securing the realm, and extending these practices to local communities. Thus all under Heaven follow the principles of ritual without departing from them and observe its forms without altering them. Only when guiding principles are established, regulations set forth, and both weighty and lesser matters properly accommodated can these be handed down without end. Such are the gradations, measures, and patterned forms of ritual.

But when cold and heat fail to arrive at their appointed times, the four seasons lose their order, mountains collapse and rivers run dry, birds and plants perish prematurely, human relationships become disordered, laws and regulations proliferate in confusion, heterodox teachings run rampant, and acts of violence arise together—these are the utter ruin and gravest corruption of ritual, their disturbances and repercussions impossible to halt [?].

The sage holds fast to the mean of Heaven and Earth and establishes constant norms for the people. Through sustaining and nurturing both the inward and the outward, he fully realizes equilibrium and harmony alike. He unites Heaven and Earth into one body and gathers people and things into his own person; thus the foundation of ritual is established. The myriad phenomena differ in form but share a common efficacy; past and present differ in time but share a common principle; the many kings differ in their laws but share a common spiritual potency. Thus the functioning of ritual proceeds from the sage himself. He fully comprehends its finest subtleties without admixture, embraces both its patterned form and its substance without omission, and fully develops its manifest arrangements, responding broadly and fittingly to every particular circumstance. Thus the measured forms of ritual become manifest through him. He takes advantage of an occasion for renewal without opposing the times, comprehends what is appropriate amid change without forcing the course of transformation, and exercises his talent for creating institutions without the manifold complications of constraint, resistance, obstruction, and evasion. Thus the means by which ritual reverses decline and restores correctness are deployed through him without exhaustion.

Hence he brings Heaven and Earth into their proper places and nurtures the myriad things. Without going beyond his hall and its steps, he achieves the work of ordering and completing, assisting and supporting the processes of Heaven and Earth, because his way of retaining or reforming, adopting or rejecting, and shaping institutions is complete. title: 嘉靖三十一年應天府鄉試錄
text:
會通以行典禮根本有據體貌有因嚴而不犯
尊而不抗莫非禮之體也財物以爲用貴賤以
爲文多少以爲異範圍而不過彌縫而有倫中
和之情流通而不間品式之制詳明而可觀莫
非禮之用也其宜隆而弗殺也則繁其文理合
其情用而不苟其宜殺而弗隆也則簡其文理
省其情用而不過從道而不從其俗任理而不
任其情使內外表裏竝行而不悖上下四方曲
折而盡數英華有質而不蕩光輝有實而不越
===
裕于中而盛于外中立無倚降殺相乗莫非理
之品節文章也損之有度而不嗇益之有制而
不侈去其太甚而不失其中矜其不能而不盡
其情其拯壞捄弊莫非禮之恊中時措之大權
也禮之本聖人植之而益嚴禮之用聖人推之
而益廣禮之品節文章聖人裁化之而益當禮
之弊且壞聖人割裁拯捄之而益善于是乎道
法之在于天地萬物者在聖人矣聖人固道之
主理之會中之極也天地萬物之命也百行五

punctuated: 會通以行典禮，根本有據，體貌有因，嚴而不犯，尊而不抗，莫非禮之體也。財物以爲用，貴賤以爲文，多少以爲異，範圍而不過，彌縫而有倫，中和之情流通而不間，品式之制詳明而可觀，莫非禮之用也。其宜隆而弗殺也，則繁其文理，合其情用而不苟；其宜殺而弗隆也，則簡其文理，省其情用而不過。從道而不從其俗，任理而不任其情，使內外表裏竝行而不悖，上下四方曲折而盡數，英華有質而不蕩，光輝有實而不越，裕于中而盛于外，中立無倚，降殺相乗，莫非理之品節文章也。損之有度而不嗇，益之有制而不侈，去其太甚而不失其中，矜其不能而不盡其情，其拯壞捄弊，莫非禮之恊中時措之大權也。禮之本，聖人植之而益嚴；禮之用，聖人推之而益廣；禮之品節文章，聖人裁化之而益當；禮之弊且壞，聖人割裁拯捄之而益善。于是乎道法之在于天地萬物者，在聖人矣。聖人固道之主，理之會，中之極也，天地萬物之命也，百行五
translation_en: …their convergences and interconnections, so as to put canonical rites into practice. Their foundations have firm grounds, and their outward forms have precedents; they are solemn without being overbearing, venerable without being aloof. All these constitute the substance of ritual. Material goods furnish its resources; distinctions of rank furnish its patterned forms; greater and lesser quantities establish its differences. It sets bounds without excess and fills gaps in an orderly manner. The feelings of equilibrium and harmony circulate without interruption, and the regulations governing grades and forms are detailed, clear, and worthy of contemplation. All these constitute the operation of ritual. Where elaboration rather than reduction is appropriate, its patterned forms are made more complex, fitting their practical application to the circumstances without carelessness. Where reduction rather than elaboration is appropriate, its patterned forms are simplified, curtailing their practical application to the circumstances without excess. Follow the Way rather than prevailing customs; rely on principle rather than personal feelings. Thus the inner and outer, the surface and what lies beneath, proceed together without conflict; above and below, throughout the four quarters, every intricacy receives its full measure. Splendor has substance and does not become unrestrained; brilliance has a solid basis and does not overstep its bounds. There is abundance within and flourishing expression without; one stands centered, inclining to neither side, while gradations of reduction support one another. All these are the graded articulations and patterned expressions of principle. Reduce with measure, without stinginess; augment within limits, without extravagance. Remove what is excessive without losing the mean; show compassion for what people cannot do, without fully indulging their feelings. Such efforts to rescue what has fallen into ruin and remedy abuses all exemplify ritual’s great discretionary power to accord with the mean and act appropriately to the time. The sages establish the foundation of ritual, making it still more august; they extend its operation, making it still broader; they shape and transform its graded articulations and patterned expressions, making them still more fitting; where ritual suffers abuses and decay, they prune, regulate, rescue, and remedy it, making it still better. Thus the Way and its standards, which reside in Heaven, Earth, and the myriad things, reside in the sages. The sages are indeed the masters of the Way, the gathering place of principle, and the ultimate standard of the mean. They are the very life of Heaven, Earth, and the myriad things; the hundred forms of conduct and the Five…

text:
常之原也治亂存亡之所視其從違以出焉者
也故郊社禘嘗袞冕宮室大路越席龍旗九斿
寢兕持虎蛟韅絲幠彌龍行于朝廷宗廟之上
至尊而不可踰者也朝覲會同師田學校燕射
冠婚城郭溝池度量權衡服食交親用于邦國
鄉黨之間達之天下之大百姓咸由而古今所
同然者也征伐四夷誅鋤强暴流放邪淫通于
變故不可已而後用之者也是莫非聖人成法
之所效也順其軌不見其異由其道不見其同
===
師其意不見其不足盡其法不見其有餘章成
物理通行而無牽合僻詖之陋此成法之所以
盡善盡美儀訓後世而不可失者也其善者賞
之使之周旋而不失依據而不違其惡者繩之
使之執守而不犯趨避而不入故能通天之道
合地之紀立人之極陰陽順軌山川奠位親義
序別信之道明内中國外四夷之防立忠信愛
敬篤近舉遠之義備親疎貴賤儀文體貌之理
盛至德潛孚至教光被與民守之而不亂安之

punctuated:
常之原也，治亂存亡之所視其從違以出焉者也。故郊社禘嘗、袞冕宮室、大路越席、龍旗九斿、寢兕持虎、蛟韅絲幠彌龍，行于朝廷宗廟之上，至尊而不可踰者也。朝覲會同、師田學校、燕射冠婚、城郭溝池、度量權衡、服食交親，用于邦國鄉黨之間，達之天下之大，百姓咸由，而古今所同然者也。征伐四夷、誅鋤强暴、流放邪淫，通于變故，不可已而後用之者也。是莫非聖人成法之所效也。順其軌，不見其異；由其道，不見其同；師其意，不見其不足；盡其法，不見其有餘。章成物理，通行而無牽合僻詖之陋。此成法之所以盡善盡美，儀訓後世而不可失者也。
其善者賞之，使之周旋而不失，依據而不違；其惡者繩之，使之執守而不犯，趨避而不入。故能通天之道，合地之紀，立人之極。陰陽順軌，山川奠位，親義序別信之道明，内中國外四夷之防立，忠信愛敬、篤近舉遠之義備，親疎貴賤、儀文體貌之理盛。至德潛孚，至教光被，與民守之而不亂，安之
translation_en:
…the source of the constant virtues. Order or disorder, preservation or ruin, arise according to whether this is followed or transgressed. Thus the suburban sacrifices to Heaven, the sacrifices to the soil, the di and chang ancestral sacrifices; ceremonial robes and caps, palaces and chambers; the great state carriage and rush mats; dragon banners with nine streamers; recumbent rhinoceroses and grasped tigers [?], dragon-adorned harness straps, silk coverings, and ornamental dragons [?]—these are employed at court and in the ancestral temples, supremely venerable and admitting no overstepping. Court audiences and assemblies of rulers, military expeditions and hunts, schools, banquets and archery ceremonies, cappings and marriages, city walls and moats, measures and balances, clothing and food, and relations with kin: these are employed throughout the states and local communities and extended across the vast realm. All the people follow them, and they have been alike acknowledged in antiquity and the present. Campaigns against the peoples of the four quarters, the execution and eradication of the violent, and the banishment of the depraved are responses to extraordinary circumstances, employed only when unavoidable. All these manifest the established institutions of the sages. Follow their tracks, and no divergence is apparent; proceed along their way, and no sameness is apparent; take their intent as a model, and no inadequacy is apparent; fully carry out their rules, and no excess is apparent. Patterns are completed and things put in order; these institutions operate universally, without the defects of forced accommodation or distorted reasoning. This is why the established institutions are wholly good and wholly beautiful, serving as models and instruction for later generations that must never be lost.
Reward those who are good, so that in all their dealings they do not fall short, and in relying on these institutions they do not depart from them. Discipline those who are wicked, so that they hold fast to them without transgression and shun wrongdoing without entering into it. Thus it is possible to accord with the Way of Heaven, conform to the ordering principles of Earth, and establish the highest standard for humanity. Yin and yang follow their proper courses; mountains and rivers are settled in their places. The principles of affection, righteousness, precedence, distinction, and trustworthiness become clear. The boundary that places the central states within and the peoples of the four quarters without is established. The duties of loyalty, trustworthiness, love, respect, devotion to those nearby, and advancement of those far away are fully realized. The principles governing closer and more distant kin, noble and humble rank, ceremonial forms, and appropriate bearing flourish. Perfect virtue quietly wins trust, and perfect instruction spreads its radiance everywhere. Together with the people, one upholds these institutions without disorder and rests content in them…

□□凝天下，熙熙然歸之大化之域者，禮之所由成也。故曰：「衡縣而輕重征矣，繩墨陳而曲直分矣，規矩設而方圓辨矣，禮法定而邪詐阻、美盛彰矣。」夫禮成而民志定者，持循之有方也；法張而民行制者，抑防之有要也。持循在，則民守之而不忍棄；抑防嚴，則民畏之而不敢違。金科玉條，垂諸百世而善者也。是道也，聖人安焉而有常，君子守之而不失，百姓由之而不知。安焉，天道也；守之、由之，人道也。天之道，自然之中也；人之道，當然之極也。當然者，理道之則；自然者，神化之原。是故以道治天下，不失聖人之成法，亦在乎以人而合諸天。

translation_en:
…[two illegible characters] bring stability to All under Heaven [?], so that all joyfully enter the realm of great transformation: this is what ritual accomplishes. Thus it is said: “Once the balance is suspended, lightness and heaviness become evident; once the marking line is laid out, crookedness and straightness are distinguished; once compass and square are set out, squareness and roundness are discerned; once ritual and law are established, wickedness and deceit are checked, and beauty and excellence become manifest.” When ritual is established and the people’s purposes become settled, it is because there is a proper method for maintaining observance. When laws are promulgated and the people’s conduct is regulated, it is because restraint and prevention grasp what is essential. When observance is maintained, the people uphold these standards and cannot bear to abandon them; when restraints are strict, the people stand in awe of them and dare not transgress. These golden statutes and jade rules remain good through a hundred generations. In this Way, sages rest at ease and remain constant; gentlemen uphold it without departing from it; and the common people follow it without knowing it. Resting at ease in it is the Way of Heaven; upholding and following it is the human Way. The Way of Heaven is the mean inherent in what is naturally so; the human Way is the ultimate standard of what ought to be. What ought to be is the norm of principle and the Way; what is naturally so is the source of numinous transformation. Thus, governing All under Heaven through the Way without departing from the sages’ established laws also depends on bringing the human into accord with Heaven.

Memorial

A congratulatory memorial composed in the role of the court officials upon the successful completion of the campaign, following an imperial edict dispatching General-in-Chief Xu Da and Left Associate General-in-Chief Li Wenzhong to lead an army to pacify the desert.〔Third year of Hongwu, 1370〕

Xu Ruji

Examiner Guo, Compiler, comments: “It extols the imperial plans and fully sets forth their excellence—an accomplishment beyond the reach of ordinary students of the classics. It merits selection.”

Feathered military dispatches race across the vast desert, relayed by signals [?]; armored troops shake the Tianshan Mountains, flashing like lightning. An exalted commission confers independent military command, and imperial might sweeps the rank stench from the northern desert. News of victory is presented to the central government, and imperial achievements bring civilization to the darkness of remote wilderness. At watchposts throughout the six frontier regions, beacon smoke subsides; within the realm’s boundaries, Hu and Yue are united as one household. Vital influence flows freely throughout the world, and achievements stand distinguished beyond the frontiers.
We reverently consider that Your Majesty the Emperor leads all mankind in divine sagacity and surpasses all others in wisdom and courage. Wielding the yellow battle-axe to direct campaigns, you marshaled the tiger-like troops of Chuyang; holding the red talisman that inaugurated your mandate, you established the magnificent foundations of your rule at Jianye. By honoring worthy men, you won the allegiance of outstanding talents; by attacking the violent, you stripped rival strongmen of their usurped titles. You crushed the sharp spearhead of mighty Han, and flags of surrender fluttered over the waters of Poyang Lake. You stormed the strong fortifications of powerful Wu, and its warships disappeared from the waves of Zhenze. Then you led a detached force into the western lands and raised your great banners over the Central Plain. At Bian and Luo you displayed your military strength, assembling three thousand soldiers like those of Mao and Pu. At ‘Chang Ying Peng’ [?] you raised troops and took possession of Qing and Qi’s rivers and mountains, whose defenses gave the strength of twelve men against two. Swiftly you came to the plains of Ji and raised your standards, pressing straight on to the outskirts of Yan…

translation_en: …and set up the war drums. Men and women cast off the left-fastened garments of three dynasties, eagerly bringing vessels of drink to welcome the army; the rivers and plains returned to the China of immemorial antiquity, and the baleful presence of the Jie vanished from streets and markets. Before the lofty walls were attacked, the army’s reputation alone terrified their ruler and ministers. Yet the desperate enemy was not pursued: allowed to move north, their people were preserved intact. How could they, scarcely released from the hunters’ nets, suddenly leap up in fury like a mantis confronting a chariot wheel? They murdered and oppressed the loyal and good, like wasps and scorpions still bent on poisonous stings; they raided and plundered the borderlands, like jackals and wolves still snarling and drooling with greed. These sinister bands fled and hid at will in three directions, and from their crafty lairs brazenly harried an entire region. How could these vile spirits, already near destruction, sustain a hundred years of barbarian rule? These unrestrained remnants of the defeated again pressed the royal army into a campaign like that of the Sixth Month. The commander set his chariot in motion: the army had just grounds for taking the field. Officers and soldiers grasped the mounting cords of their chariots: this undertaking could not be avoided. Their conduct of strategy benefited from plans already perfected in the imperial councils; thus, in their wrath against the enemy, they repeatedly brought victories to the commander’s gate. The mighty bows shot in every direction, and righteousness stirred the whole army to unity of purpose. The imperial battle-axe extended its authority afar, and the assembled officers obeyed commands as readily as an arm follows its owner’s will. The justice of the undertaking amply demonstrated the support of men; the barbarians’ arrogance met, it seemed, with destruction decreed by Heaven. Advancing from Tongguan to strike Dingxi, the main host swept forward with the ease of splitting bamboo; driving straight from Huling into the lands north of the desert, the left army ultimately displayed its might by destroying the enemy’s nest. Wind and sand carried the army’s renown over ten thousand li; grass and trees trembled with the killing force that filled the three border regions. The chieftains of Gaochang and Baohan submitted to capture with silk cords crossed about their necks; the various divisions of Kaiping and Yingchang hastened in carts of surrender [?] to be bound. The precious vessels were inventoried first…

title: 嘉靖三十一年應天府鄉試錄
text:
□□□□□□□□□□□□之姫嬙耻雪百王
往代既舒其積憤
勳垂千古遺黎亦快於前讐豈徒章諸夏之
奇功實以遏殘胡之隱禍從此
昇平無事必今勞可免後艱固知薄伐有煩
將永佚其存玆舉招哉得絕逆除凶之道
允矣非窮兵黷武之謀臣某等謬參
禁省之末僚莫贊
宸幃之密畫虜情如見歎
===

命武威揚而諸醜服桓桓績載於無前

獻琛掃旄頭以靖八荒椎結效三危之格羽

靈圖新曆數於萬年臣等無任瞻

translation_en:
…[Twelve illegible characters] the palace women [?]. The disgrace of a hundred kings has been avenged, and bygone dynasties have at last discharged their accumulated indignation. Your achievements will endure for a thousand ages, and the surviving people likewise rejoice in vengeance for former wrongs. This does more than manifest the extraordinary achievements of the Chinese realm: it also forestalls the latent danger posed by the remaining Hu. Henceforth there will be peace and freedom from trouble; present exertions will surely avert future difficulties. We know that this punitive expedition has required toil, yet lasting repose will depend upon this undertaking. Admirable indeed [?]: it accords with the way of cutting off rebellion and eliminating evil. Truly, it is no scheme for exhausting the armies and recklessly pursuing war.

We, your servants So-and-so and the others, undeservedly hold places among the lowest officials of the palace administration and have contributed nothing to the confidential plans formed within your imperial curtains. The enemy’s circumstances seemed plainly visible: we marvel that an emperor possesses true insight [?]. The army’s discipline shared in transgression [?]; we rejoice that commanders and officers all obeyed their orders. Your martial might has spread abroad, and the vile multitude has submitted; your valiant achievements stand recorded as unprecedented. Your luminous virtue is carefully maintained, and the peoples of the four quarters come in submission; your glorious accomplishments shine forth throughout a realm brought into order. Joining the assembled ranks [?], we dance together, reverently clapping and stamping [?] as we raise our voices in praise.

We humbly wish that your enterprise may blaze like the expedition in the Book of Changes’ Li hexagram, and your achievements shine like the campaign in its Jin hexagram. Establish the four extremities of the world with the great turtle’s legs, so that tribute bearers may come over mountains and seas, through nine stages of interpretation, to offer precious treasures. Sweep away the Hairy Head constellation of war and pacify the eight wildernesses, so that those who wear their hair in topknots may emulate the people of Sanwei, won over by the dance with feathered plumes. May your magnificent mandate bring renewed splendor to the unified carriage gauges and written script throughout the six zones of allegiance; may your sacred imperial design renew the succession of sovereign rule for ten thousand years. We, your servants, cannot contain ourselves as we gaze upward…

title: 嘉靖三十一年應天府鄉試錄
text:
考試官右中允尹批是作能鋪張我
二祖開創之盛
皇上繼述之隆末意尤見忠懇必非凡士也取之
聖人舉天下之事必觀時而勢有不可失
者焉建天下之業必察勢而時有不可違
者焉觀時者與天不得其勢以輔之則雖
順而難成察勢者與地不得其時以協之
則雖據而無功舉不失勢可以興事作不
違時可以定業□□人所以成久安長治
===
之道遺諸千萬□□墜缺者也昔我
太祖高皇帝定鼎金陵決策於大勳未集之先
蓋觀天下之時不失其勢矣
成祖文皇帝考卜燕京定議於內難旣靖之後
蓋察天下之勢不違其時矣夫開國建都
包四海之形要興事定業兼百王之功美
自生民以來孰有能過我
二祖之盛者哉執事猥問承學之士敢不究罄
臆說以對上古聖人君世宰物其事難述

punctuated:
考試官右中允尹批：是作能鋪張我二祖開創之盛、皇上繼述之隆，末意尤見忠懇，必非凡士也，取之。
聖人舉天下之事，必觀時，而勢有不可失者焉；建天下之業，必察勢，而時有不可違者焉。觀時者與天，不得其勢以輔之，則雖順而難成；察勢者與地，不得其時以協之，則雖據而無功。舉不失勢，可以興事；作不違時，可以定業。□□人所以成久安長治之道，遺諸千萬□□墜缺者也。昔我太祖高皇帝定鼎金陵，決策於大勳未集之先，蓋觀天下之時，不失其勢矣。成祖文皇帝考卜燕京，定議於內難旣靖之後，蓋察天下之勢，不違其時矣。夫開國建都，包四海之形要；興事定業，兼百王之功美。自生民以來，孰有能過我二祖之盛者哉？執事猥問承學之士，敢不究罄臆說以對？上古聖人君世宰物，其事難述
translation_en:
Examiner Yin, Right Mentor, comments: This composition fully sets forth the splendor of our two ancestral emperors’ founding achievements and the grandeur of His Majesty’s continuation of their work. Its concluding ideas especially reveal loyalty and sincerity. This must be an exceptional scholar. Select him.
When sages undertake the affairs of the realm, they invariably consider the times; yet there are strategic advantages they must not let slip. When they establish enduring enterprises for the realm, they invariably examine the configuration of circumstances; yet there are demands of the times they must not contravene. Considering the times accords with Heaven, but without favorable circumstances to assist, success is difficult even when one follows Heaven. Examining strategic circumstances accords with Earth, but without the appropriate time to complement them, even possession of a strategic position brings no accomplishment. Undertaking action without losing strategic advantage enables one to initiate affairs; acting without contravening the times enables one to establish enduring achievements. This is how … [?] bring about lasting peace and enduring good government, bequeathing it for countless generations without impairment [?]. In former times, our Emperor Taizu Gao established his capital at Jinling, deciding upon this policy before his great achievement was complete. He thus considered the times throughout the realm and did not lose their strategic advantages. Emperor Chengzu Wen examined the auspices for establishing his capital at Yanjing, settling the matter after the internal troubles had been quelled. He thus examined the strategic circumstances of the realm and did not contravene the times. In founding the state and establishing its capitals, they encompassed the strategically vital terrain within the Four Seas; in initiating affairs and establishing enduring achievements, they united the glorious accomplishments of a hundred kings. Since humankind first existed, who has surpassed the splendor of our two ancestral emperors? You, honored examiners, have graciously questioned scholars who have inherited the teachings. How could I dare not exhaust my humble understanding in reply? The sages of high antiquity ruled the world and governed all things; their deeds are difficult to recount …

title: 嘉靖三十一年應天府鄉試錄

迄于宋氏舊京錯峙大抵多先王往治之

都斯豈惟山川形險是擇哉蓋亦帝王各
因其初迹不可迄改焉是故作於殷周之
前非多匹夫遜位四侯造邦者邪德之所
===

為安矣興於秦漢之後非多奮績驅攘併

translation_en:
…in detail. The ages of Tang and Yu and the Three Dynasties are recorded in the Book of Odes and the Book of Documents. Of all those who gained the realm, was there any who did not observe Heaven’s timing? The past deeds associated with famous capitals are clearly set forth in historical records. Of all those who preserved the realm, was there any who did not examine the strategic configuration of the land? Pingyang and Puban were established in Jin and Ji; Boyuan and Fengyi lay in Yong and Yu. From Qin and Han down to the Song, former capitals stood scattered across the land, mostly on sites where earlier kings had governed. The Grand Astrologer said: “The Three He are the center of Heaven and Earth, where kings established their capitals in succession.” Was this merely a matter of choosing naturally defensible mountains and rivers? It was also because each emperor or king followed the circumstances of his beginnings and could not wholly change them.

Thus, among those who arose before Yin and Zhou, were there not many cases of abdication to commoners and of the ‘four lords’ founding states [?]? How could they alone change the [illegible] where their virtue first arose? They determined orientations and laid out the countryside; the realm found security in submitting to them. Among those who arose from Qin and Han onward, were there not many who achieved distinction through expulsion and conquest, uniting divided territories? How could they alone abandon the people among whom their achievements had been won? Thus they controlled defensible positions and guarded strategic points, and later generations followed their example to secure their rule.

A great merchant pursuing the profits of routes reaching in all directions must seek a settled place to store his goods: this illustrates that those skilled in timing have resources on which to draw. A skilled forester, gathering the catch of a hunt driven from three sides, must reckon whether the ‘fuge’ can be deployed [?]: this illustrates that those skilled in using circumstances have favorable conditions to follow. Thus, in gaining the realm before it has been unified, nothing is more important than understanding timing. Yet unless one draws on strategic advantages as a resource, gains cannot make good losses, and at the outset it is difficult to join in the undertaking; victories cannot offset defeats, and in bringing it to completion it is difficult…

title: 嘉靖三十一年應天府鄉試錄
text:
圖終也觀順逆之形以决取舍之效非天
下至聖其孰能辨之惟我
太祖取濠定滁躍馬和陽乘其方張之氣天下
可亟取矣乃卷旆偏引南顧而議金陵焉
夫當元季俶擾生民罹塗炭之苦羣雄相
噬無有以弔伐爲心者得
聖人而出主之非勞民之易爲仁邪故夫知時
之難得而易失不可不圖其勢也於是引
舟巢湖舉太平□□慶出入百戰以定養
===
兵息民之計則天下之資具焉故首殲
勁漢通江沔之上游次拔强吳收甌越之
全饒兵甲足而糗粮峙整師中原四方不
足平爾此非先得乎時而能取勢以爲之
輔哉故曰舉事者必觀時然勢不可失也
夫長江巨浸不殊三國之天險浚隍危堞
不增六代之地利何王業所成相遠也蓋
盛衰要於人事昔之僭號一隅者可得而
同論邪故

translation_en:
…to plan its completion. To observe whether circumstances favor or oppose an undertaking and thereby determine the consequences of adopting or abandoning a course—who but the greatest sage under Heaven could discern this?

Our Taizu alone captured Hao and secured Chu, riding forth at Heyang. With his momentum then rising, it seemed that all under Heaven could quickly be taken. Yet he furled his banners and diverted his advance, looking south and making plans for Jinling. Amid the turmoil at the end of the Yuan, the people suffered as though mired in mud and burning coals, while rival warlords devoured one another. None took to heart the duty to console the afflicted and punish the guilty. When a sage emerged to rule them, was it not easy to practice benevolence toward an exhausted people? Thus, knowing that the right moment is difficult to obtain and easily lost, one must also plan how to secure a favorable strategic position. He therefore brought boats from Chaohu, took Taiping and …qing [?], and fought a hundred battles, thereby establishing a plan to sustain his troops and give the people respite. The resources for gaining all under Heaven were thus complete.

First he annihilated mighty Han, opening the upper reaches of the Yangzi and Mian rivers; next he overthrew powerful Wu, acquiring all the wealth of Ou and Yue. With ample arms and armor and stockpiles of provisions, he marshaled his armies in the Central Plain; pacifying the four quarters was then no great task. Was this not a case of first seizing the right moment and then securing strategic advantages to support it? Thus it is said: “Those who undertake great affairs must observe the times, yet must not forfeit strategic advantage.”

The vast waters of the Yangzi offered no different natural barrier from that of the Three Kingdoms; deep moats and lofty battlements afforded no greater advantage of terrain than those of the Six Dynasties. Why, then, were their achievements in founding royal dominion so far apart? Surely rise and decline depend ultimately on human affairs. Could those of earlier times who presumptuously assumed sovereign titles in a single corner of the realm be discussed on the same terms? Therefore…

title: 嘉靖三十一年應天府鄉試錄
text:
聖祖述閱江樓記以爲非古之金陵亦非六朝
之建業也蓋先巳明此矣乃當時御史胡
子祺者特疏請改都關中是其言非無可
采然徒知陳說往代推創造基本當擇乎
形勢而不知時有不可違者夫古人立國
必就功業之所厚以建久治則上不勞而
下易集昔漢高帝功始定秦秦人無不願
得其王者高帝乃舍之王洛陽焉婁敬諫
曰陛下豈欲比□□室哉漢取天下與周
===
異也夫我
聖祖興吳不猶漢高之起秦邪況其時關陝承
擴廓思齊之亂王澤漬濡未浹也江南貢
賦運濟方艱强而議都其能免新造之勞
傷乎故子祺疏入不報非諱其言之左也
一入其說則事有不可但巳者夫利害本
末之權惟達於時順之士能明之故舉不
失時可以興事而子祺則或未之及也若
夫守天下於旣定之後莫貴乎審勢然非
